o: opens into the pterygopalatine fossa

Foramen rotundum runs forward from the middle cranial fossa and opens into the upper part of the pterygopalatine fossa. The maxillary nerve passes through it.
The pterygoid canal opens into the same fossa, below and medial to it.
transmits the accessory meningeal artery

The accessory meningeal artery enters the skull through foramen ovale. Last's says its chief supply goes to the trigeminal ganglion.
Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery; foramen rotundum transmits only V2 and small emissary veins.
transmits the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve

The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve is the only significant content of foramen rotundum.
V1 leaves through the superior orbital fissure and V3 through foramen ovale.
lies medial to the anterior clinoid process

Foramen rotundum lies in the root of the greater wing below the medial end of the superior orbital fissure, inferolateral to the anterior clinoid process. The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus attaches at its lateral margin.
The opening that lies medial to the anterior clinoid process is the optic canal.

questions.s: The zygomatic bone articulates with the
o: frontal bone

The frontal process of the zygomatic bone meets the zygomatic process of the frontal bone at the frontozygomatic suture, a palpable landmark on the lateral orbital margin.
It is a reference point for pterion and burr-hole surface markings.
temporal bone

The temporal process of the zygomatic bone meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch.
The arch gives origin to masseter.
maxilla

The zygomatic bone articulates with the zygomatic process of the maxilla, forming the anterior pillar of the arch and part of the orbital floor and rim.
This joint is disrupted in "tripod" fractures.
greater wing of the sphenoid

The orbital surface of the zygomatic bone articulates with the greater wing of the sphenoid in the lateral wall of the orbit.
The zygomatic bone articulates with these four bones only: frontal, temporal, maxilla and sphenoid.

questions.t: Foramina of the middle cranial fossa
o: It lies in the greater wing of the sphenoid, below the medial end of the superior orbital fissure

Foramen rotundum pierces the root of the greater wing of the sphenoid just below the medial end of the superior orbital fissure.
It runs forward, not downward.
It opens anteriorly into the pterygopalatine fossa

The maxillary nerve passes forward through foramen rotundum into the upper part of the pterygopalatine fossa.
There it gives branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
It transmits the maxillary nerve and the middle meningeal artery

Foramen rotundum transmits only the maxillary nerve (with small emissary veins). The middle meningeal artery passes through foramen spinosum.
"Rotundum: V2; ovale: V3; spinosum: middle meningeal artery."
It transmits the nerve of the pterygoid canal

The nerve of the pterygoid canal runs in the pterygoid canal, which lies below and medial to foramen rotundum.
Both open into the pterygopalatine fossa.

questions.t: Foramina of the middle cranial fossa
questions.s: Structures passing through the foramen ovale include the:
o: Lesser petrosal nerve

The lesser petrosal nerve usually leaves the skull through foramen ovale (sometimes through the small canaliculus innominatus) to reach the otic ganglion.
It carries IX fibres for the parotid.
Accessory meningeal artery

The accessory meningeal artery, from the maxillary or middle meningeal artery, enters the skull through foramen ovale.
It supplies the trigeminal ganglion and dura.
Nervus spinosus

The nervus spinosus (meningeal branch of V3) arises below the skull and re-enters through foramen spinosum with the middle meningeal artery.
Last's notes it may sometimes pass through foramen ovale, but foramen spinosum is the usual route.
Emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus to the pterygoid plexus

Emissary veins through foramen ovale connect the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus.
This is a route for infection to spread into the cavernous sinus.

questions.t: Foramina of the middle cranial fossa
o: It lies posterolateral to the foramen ovale

Foramen spinosum lies just posterolateral to foramen ovale, close to the spine of the sphenoid.
The three foramina form a curve: rotundum, ovale, spinosum.
It transmits the middle meningeal artery

The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the first part of the maxillary artery, enters the middle cranial fossa through foramen spinosum.
It then grooves the inner skull, and its anterior branch passes deep to the pterion.
It transmits the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve

The meningeal branch of V3 (nervus spinosus) accompanies the artery back into the skull through foramen spinosum.
It supplies the dura of the posterior middle fossa and the mastoid air cells.
It lies anteromedial to the spine of the sphenoid

The spine of the sphenoid lies posterolateral to the foramen, which is therefore anteromedial to it. The spine gives attachment to the sphenomandibular ligament.
Its name comes from this spine.
Articulates with the greater wing of the sphenoid

The orbital surface of the zygomatic bone articulates with the greater wing of the sphenoid, forming part of the lateral orbital wall.
Its frontal process articulates with the frontal bone.
Articulates with the lacrimal bone

The zygomatic bone articulates with four bones: frontal, sphenoid, temporal and maxilla. The lacrimal bone does not reach it.
The lacrimal bone lies in the medial wall of the orbit.
Transmits branches of the maxillary nerve through the zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal foramina

The zygomatic nerve (from V2) divides into zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal branches, which pierce the zygomatic bone through their own foramina.
They supply the skin of the cheek and temple.
Gives attachment to the masseter muscle

The superficial part of masseter arises from the zygomatic process of the maxilla and the lower border of the zygomatic arch (zygomatic bone).
The deep part arises from the deep surface of the arch.
It lies between the petrous temporal bone and the occipital bone

The jugular foramen lies at the posterior end of the petro-occipital fissure, between the jugular notches of the petrous temporal and occipital bones.
It is the largest foramen of the posterior cranial fossa after the foramen magnum.
The inferior petrosal sinus passes through its anterior part

The inferior petrosal sinus occupies the anterior compartment and joins the internal jugular vein just below the skull.
IX lies lateral to it in this compartment.
The glossopharyngeal nerve passes through its posterior part with the sigmoid sinus

Last's says two dural septa divide the foramen into three compartments. IX shares the anterior compartment with the inferior petrosal sinus. X and XI occupy the middle compartment, and the posterior compartment holds the jugular bulb (the end of the sigmoid sinus).
So IX is anterior, not posterior.
The hypoglossal nerve passes through it

The hypoglossal nerve leaves through its own hypoglossal canal, above the anterior part of the occipital condyle.
The canal lies deep and medial to the jugular foramen.
It transmits the facial nerve, the nervus intermedius and the vestibulocochlear nerve

The facial nerve, nervus intermedius and vestibulocochlear nerve, with the labyrinthine artery, enter the internal acoustic meatus.
Vestibular schwannomas arise here.
The facial nerve lies in the anterosuperior quadrant of the fundus

At the fundus the transverse crest separates the upper facial and superior vestibular areas from the lower cochlear and inferior vestibular areas. The facial nerve is anterosuperior.
"Seven up, Coke down" for the anterior quadrants.
The cochlear nerve lies in the posterosuperior quadrant

The cochlear nerve lies in the anteroinferior quadrant. The superior vestibular nerve is posterosuperior.
The inferior vestibular nerve is posteroinferior.
The labyrinthine artery is most commonly a branch of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery

Last's gives the labyrinthine artery as a branch of the basilar artery or of AICA, never of PICA.
It is an end artery; occlusion causes sudden deafness and vertigo.

questions.s: Structures passing through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring include the:
o: Nasociliary nerve

The nasociliary nerve passes within the common tendinous ring, between the two divisions of III.
It is the only branch of V1 inside the ring.
Abducent nerve

VI passes within the ring, inferolateral to the nasociliary nerve, to reach lateral rectus.
It is the lowest structure in the ring.
Superior and inferior divisions of the oculomotor nerve

Both the superior and inferior divisions of III pass within the ring.
The superior division supplies superior rectus and levator; the inferior division the other muscles.
Trochlear nerve

IV passes above (outside) the ring, together with the frontal and lacrimal nerves.
These three lie outside the muscle cone; the superior ophthalmic vein also usually passes outside.
Lies between the two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid

The optic canal is bounded by the body of the sphenoid medially and the two roots of the lesser wing above and below.
It transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery.
Transmits the ophthalmic artery, which lies above and medial to the optic nerve

In the optic canal the ophthalmic artery lies below and lateral to the optic nerve, within the dural sheath.
It crosses above the nerve later, in the orbit.
Transmits postganglionic sympathetic fibres

Postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus accompany the ophthalmic artery through the optic canal.
Some sympathetic fibres also enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Is separated from the sphenoidal sinus by bone that may be very thin

The optic canal is related medially to the sphenoidal (and sometimes posterior ethmoidal) sinus, and the bony wall between them may be very thin or deficient.
This puts the nerve at risk in endoscopic sinus surgery.

questions.s: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the:
o: Nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen

The sphenopalatine foramen, in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa, opens into the nasal cavity behind the middle meatus.
The sphenopalatine artery and nasal nerves pass through it.
Orbit through the inferior orbital fissure

The apex of the inferior orbital fissure opens into the pterygopalatine fossa, so the fossa communicates with the orbit.
V2 continues forward through this fissure as the infraorbital nerve.
Oral cavity through the greater palatine canal

The greater and lesser palatine canals lead down from the fossa to the palate (oral cavity).
The palatine nerves and vessels run through them.
Posterior cranial fossa through the pterygoid canal

The pterygoid canal opens posteriorly at the anterior wall of foramen lacerum, in the middle cranial fossa, not the posterior cranial fossa.
Foramen rotundum also links the fossa with the middle cranial fossa.
It is the H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, squamous temporal bones and greater wing of the sphenoid

The pterion is the H-shaped junction of four bones: frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid.
It lies in the temporal fossa.
It overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery

The anterior (frontal) branch of the middle meningeal artery grooves, or tunnels through, the inner surface of the skull at the pterion.
A fracture here may tear it, causing an extradural haematoma.
Its burr-hole site lies about 3 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch, behind and above the frontozygomatic suture

Last's surface marking for exposing the frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery is about 3 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch, behind and above the frontozygomatic suture.
Many other texts quote 4 cm; know both.
It overlies the junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinuses

The junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinuses lies deep to the asterion, where the parietal, occipital and mastoid temporal bones meet.
The asterion is a landmark for retrosigmoid approaches.

questions.s: Structures passing through the foramen magnum include the:
o: Hypoglossal nerves

The hypoglossal nerves leave through the hypoglossal canals, not the foramen magnum.
The canals lie above the occipital condyles.
Vertebral arteries

The vertebral arteries pierce the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and dura and enter the skull through the foramen magnum.
They join to form the basilar artery at the lower border of the pons.
Internal jugular veins

The sigmoid sinus becomes the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen.
The foramen magnum transmits no major venous trunk, though venous plexuses pass through it.
Spinal roots of the accessory nerves

The spinal roots of the accessory nerves ascend through the foramen magnum to join the cranial roots.
Last's lists the lower medulla, spinal arteries and veins, vertebral arteries and spinal accessory roots as its contents.

questions.s: On the anterior (cerebral) surface of the petrous temporal bone:
o: The arcuate eminence is produced by the superior semicircular canal

The arcuate eminence on the anterior surface of the petrous bone is raised by the underlying superior (anterior) semicircular canal.
It is a landmark in middle fossa approaches to the internal acoustic meatus.
The tegmen tympani forms the roof of the middle ear and mastoid antrum

The thin tegmen tympani roofs the tympanic cavity and the mastoid antrum, and continues forward over the canal for the auditory tube.
Middle ear infection can spread through it to cause a temporal lobe abscess or meningitis.
The hiatus for the greater petrosal nerve lies lateral to the hiatus for the lesser petrosal nerve

The hiatus for the greater petrosal nerve lies medial to (and in front of) the smaller hiatus for the lesser petrosal nerve.
Both nerves run forward and medially towards the foramen lacerum and foramen ovale respectively.
The trigeminal impression lies near the apex

The trigeminal impression lies near the apex of the petrous bone, where the trigeminal ganglion lies in Meckel's cave.
The internal carotid artery lies beneath it in the carotid canal.
In life it is closed by dense fibrous tissue and transmits no major structure

Last's says that, apart from minute emissary veins, no structure passes through the foramen lacerum from the cranial cavity to the exterior. In life its lower part is closed by dense fibrocartilage.
It is a useful point that is often asked.
The internal carotid artery passes vertically through it from the neck

The internal carotid artery enters through the carotid canal and crosses the upper part of the foramen lacerum horizontally, then turns up into the cavernous sinus. It does not traverse the foramen from below.
This is the "lacerum segment" of the artery.
The greater and deep petrosal nerves unite here to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal

The greater petrosal and deep petrosal nerves unite at the foramen lacerum to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal, which enters the canal in its anterior wall.
The combined nerve carries parasympathetic and sympathetic fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Lies between the apex of the petrous temporal bone and the body and greater wing of the sphenoid

The foramen lacerum lies between the apex of the petrous temporal bone and the body and greater wing of the sphenoid, with the basiocciput medially.
It is a jagged gap at the junction of these bones.
The sphenomandibular ligament attaches to the lingula

The lingula projects over the mandibular foramen and gives attachment to the sphenomandibular ligament, a remnant of Meckel's cartilage.
It is a landmark for inferior alveolar nerve block.
The superior mental (genial) spines give origin to geniohyoid

The superior genial tubercles (mental spines) give origin to genioglossus. Geniohyoid arises from the inferior tubercles.
"Genioglossus above, geniohyoid below," following their positions in the floor of the mouth.
The lateral pterygoid inserts into the pterygoid fovea on the front of the neck of the mandible

Last's describes the two heads of lateral pterygoid lying edge to edge and forming a thick tendon inserted into the pterygoid fovea on the front of the neck of the mandible (with some fibres to the disc). They draw the condyle and disc forward down the articular tubercle.
It is the main opener of the mouth.
In the adult the mental foramen lies midway between the upper and lower borders below the second premolar

In the dentate adult the mental foramen lies midway between the upper and lower borders of the mandible, below the second premolar.
In infants it lies near the lower border; in the edentulous elderly near the upper border, because the alveolar margin is absorbed.
Gives attachment to the middle constrictor along the greater horn and lesser horn

The middle constrictor arises from the upper border of the greater horn of the hyoid, the lesser horn and the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament.
So it fans back from the hyoid around the pharynx.
Has its lesser horns derived from the third pharyngeal arch

The lesser horns and upper part of the body of the hyoid come from the second pharyngeal arch. The greater horns and lower body come from the third arch.
Second arch = Reichert's cartilage (stylohyoid ligament, lesser horn).
Is separated from the thyrohyoid membrane by a bursa

The thyrohyoid membrane attaches to the upper border of the back of the hyoid body, and a bursa lies between the membrane and the posterior surface of the body.
This allows the larynx to slide up behind the hyoid during swallowing.
Gives attachment to the stylohyoid ligament at the tip of the greater horn

The stylohyoid ligament attaches to the lesser horn of the hyoid, not the greater horn.
Both are second-arch derivatives.

questions.s: In the skull of the newborn:
o: The mastoid process is absent and the facial nerve is relatively unprotected as it emerges from the stylomastoid foramen

The mastoid process develops only after the second year, so in the newborn the facial nerve emerges from the stylomastoid foramen superficially, covered only by fibres of sternocleidomastoid.
A postauricular incision in an infant can easily cut it.
The mastoid antrum is absent

The internal ear, middle ear and mastoid antrum are fully developed at birth.
Only the mastoid process and air cells develop later.
The vault contains no cancellous diploe

At birth the vault bones are a single layer of compact bone, with no cancellous diploe.
The diploe develops later in childhood.
The anterior fontanelle closes at about 18 months

Last's says the anterior fontanelle closes at about 18 months and the posterior fontanelle by the end of the first year.
A bulging anterior fontanelle in an infant indicates raised intracranial pressure.
The tympanic membrane is almost of adult size

At birth the tympanic membrane is nearly of adult size, though it faces more downward.
The external meatus is short and mostly cartilaginous.
The mandibular fossa is deep and faces directly forward

At birth the mandibular fossa is shallow and faces slightly laterally. It deepens and turns forward with development.
The articular tubercle is also undeveloped.
The maxillary sinus is a narrow slit in the medial wall of the maxilla

At birth the maxillary sinus is a narrow slit in the medial wall of the maxilla. It enlarges rapidly once the permanent teeth begin to erupt, at about six years.
So sinusitis of the maxillary sinus is rare in infants.
The two halves of the frontal bone are united by a fused metopic suture

At birth the frontal bone is in two halves. Last's says the metopic suture usually unites in the second year, though it may persist.
A persistent metopic suture can be mistaken for a fracture.
The falx cerebri attaches to the crista galli

The anterior end of the falx cerebri attaches to the crista galli of the ethmoid.
The superior sagittal sinus begins near here.
The anterior ethmoidal nerve crosses the cribriform plate before entering the nasal cavity beside the crista galli

The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters the cranial cavity from the orbit through the anterior ethmoidal foramen, runs extradurally on the cribriform plate, then descends through a slit beside the crista galli into the nose.
It is the only V1 branch to run within the cranial cavity.
The foramen caecum may transmit an emissary vein from the nose to the superior sagittal sinus

Last's says the foramen caecum is usually a blind pit plugged by the falx. Only in about 1 percent does a patent vein connect the nasal veins with the superior sagittal sinus.
So the statement "may transmit" is correct.
Its floor is formed entirely by the orbital plates of the frontal bone

The floor of the anterior cranial fossa is formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, and the lesser wings and front of the body (jugum) of the sphenoid.
Not by the frontal bone alone.

questions.s: Concerning the sphenoid bone and sella turcica:
o: The tentorium cerebelli's free border attaches to the anterior clinoid process

The free margin of the tentorium runs forward to the anterior clinoid process, while the attached margin ends at the posterior clinoid process, so the two margins cross.
III and IV pierce the dura near this crossing.
The pituitary gland is separated from the sphenoidal sinus by the floor of the hypophysial fossa

The pituitary gland is separated from the sphenoidal sinus below only by the floor of the hypophysial fossa.
This relationship is the basis of the trans-sphenoidal approach.
The diaphragma sellae is pierced by the infundibulum

The diaphragma sellae roofs the hypophysial fossa and is pierced centrally by the infundibulum (pituitary stalk).
A suprasellar tumour must push it up.
The optic chiasma lies directly within the hypophysial fossa

The optic chiasma lies above the diaphragma sellae, usually above and slightly behind the tuberculum sellae, not within the fossa.
A pituitary tumour must grow upward through the diaphragma to reach it.
Lies between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the orbital surface of the maxilla

The inferior orbital fissure separates the lateral wall of the orbit (greater wing of the sphenoid) from the floor (maxilla and orbital process of the palatine).
It leads back into the pterygopalatine fossa.
Transmits the zygomatic nerve

The zygomatic branch of V2 enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure.
It carries lacrimal secretomotor fibres up the lateral wall.
Transmits the infraorbital vessels and nerve

The infraorbital nerve and vessels pass through the inferior orbital fissure into the infraorbital groove and canal.
They emerge on the face at the infraorbital foramen.
Transmits the superior ophthalmic vein

The superior ophthalmic vein passes through the superior orbital fissure. Branches of the inferior ophthalmic vein may pass through the inferior fissure to the pterygoid plexus.
Superior vein, superior fissure.

questions.s: The medial wall of the orbit is formed by the:
o: Frontal process of the maxilla

The frontal process of the maxilla forms the anterior part of the medial orbital wall, including the anterior lacrimal crest.
The medial palpebral ligament attaches here.
Lacrimal bone

The lacrimal bone carries the posterior lacrimal crest and forms part of the lacrimal fossa.
Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi arises from the crest.
Orbital plate (lamina papyracea) of the ethmoid

The paper-thin orbital plate (lamina papyracea) of the ethmoid forms most of the medial wall.
Ethmoid sinus infection easily breaches it, causing orbital cellulitis.
Orbital surface of the zygomatic bone

The zygomatic bone contributes to the lateral wall and floor, not the medial wall. The body of the sphenoid completes the medial wall posteriorly.
Medial wall bones: maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, sphenoid.

questions.s: Regarding the walls of the tympanic cavity:
o: The promontory on the medial wall is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea

The promontory on the medial wall of the middle ear is formed by the basal (first) turn of the cochlea and is covered by the tympanic plexus.
The oval window lies above and behind it, the round window below and behind.
The prominence of the facial canal lies above the oval window on the medial wall

The prominence of the facial canal runs backward on the medial wall above the oval window, then turns down in the posterior wall.
The facial nerve is at risk in stapes surgery.
The floor separates the cavity from the internal carotid artery

The floor of the tympanic cavity is a thin plate separating it from the bulb of the internal jugular vein. The internal carotid artery is related to the anterior wall.
A high jugular bulb can bulge into the middle ear.
The aditus to the mastoid antrum lies in the upper part of the posterior wall

The aditus to the mastoid antrum lies in the upper part of the posterior wall, leading back from the epitympanic recess to the antrum.
Infection spreads from the middle ear to the mastoid through it.
The oculomotor and trochlear nerves lie in its lateral wall

III and IV lie in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. From above down the wall contains III, IV, V1 and V2.
Lesions of the sinus produce ophthalmoplegia with facial sensory loss.
The abducent nerve lies in the lateral wall below the ophthalmic nerve

Last's says VI lies within the sinus, lateral to and then below the internal carotid artery, not in the lateral wall.
No nerve lies medial to VI, and no nerve lies lateral to the trigeminal branches.
It drains into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses

The cavernous sinus drains posteriorly into the superior petrosal sinus (to the transverse/sigmoid) and the inferior petrosal sinus (to the internal jugular vein).
It also communicates with the pterygoid plexus and ophthalmic veins.
It receives the superficial middle cerebral vein

Last's says the superficial middle cerebral vein crosses the subarachnoid space and pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus near the emerging internal carotid artery.
This is how cavernous thrombosis can spread to the hemisphere.
Is formed by the union of the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein

The straight sinus is formed by the union of the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein, at the front of the junction of falx and tentorium.
It drains the deep venous system.
Runs in the line of attachment of the falx cerebri to the tentorium cerebelli

The straight sinus runs backward in the line of attachment of the falx cerebri to the tentorium cerebelli, to the internal occipital protuberance.
There it joins the confluence or turns into a transverse sinus.
Usually becomes continuous with the left transverse sinus

The superior sagittal sinus usually continues as the right transverse sinus, and the straight sinus as the left.
That is why the right internal jugular vein is often larger.
Slopes gently, at much less than 45 degrees, from front to back

Last's says the straight sinus slopes down steeply, at more than 45 degrees, in the intact dura.
Last's also says it receives the inferior sagittal sinus, the great cerebral vein and both basal veins at its anterior end.

questions.s: Regarding the sensory nerve supply of the cranial dura:
o: The upper surface of the tentorium cerebelli is supplied by tentorial branches of the ophthalmic nerve

Last's says the tentorial nerves of V1 arise at the front of the cavernous sinus and supply the falx, the vault dura and the upper surface of the tentorium.
The under surface of the tentorium is supplied by IX and X (and upper cervical nerves).
The dura around the margin of the foramen magnum is supplied by the upper three cervical nerves

The dura around the margin of the foramen magnum is supplied by the upper three cervical nerves. The rest of the posterior fossa dura is supplied by meningeal branches of IX and X.
This explains suboccipital pain from posterior fossa lesions.
The dura of the middle cranial fossa is supplied mainly by the facial nerve

Last's says the anterior half of the middle fossa dura is supplied by the middle meningeal nerve (V2) and the posterior half by the nervus spinosus (V3). The facial nerve does not supply the dura.
Supratentorial dura is all trigeminal.
The dura of the anterior cranial fossa receives branches of the anterior ethmoidal nerve

The anterior ethmoidal nerve and other V1 branches supply the dura of the anterior cranial fossa.
So frontal headache can arise from anterior fossa dura.
The mastoid emissary vein connects the sigmoid sinus to the posterior auricular or occipital veins

The mastoid emissary vein runs through the mastoid foramen, connecting the sigmoid sinus with the posterior auricular or occipital veins.
It may bleed briskly in mastoid surgery.
They contain valves that ensure flow is directed outward

Emissary veins are valveless, so blood can flow in either direction.
That is why scalp infection can spread to the venous sinuses.
The parietal emissary vein connects the superior sagittal sinus with veins of the scalp

The parietal emissary vein passes through the parietal foramen, connecting the superior sagittal sinus with veins of the scalp.
It is near the midline at the back of the parietal bone.
A vein through the hypoglossal canal connects the sigmoid sinus or basilar plexus with the internal jugular vein

A venous plexus in the hypoglossal canal connects the sigmoid sinus or basilar plexus with the internal jugular vein.
This is one of several emissary routes at the skull base.
The hypoglossal canal lies above the anterior part of the occipital condyle

The hypoglossal canal pierces the occipital bone above the anterior part of each occipital condyle.
XII leaves through it.
The condylar canal, when present, transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus

The posterior condylar canal, in the condylar fossa behind the condyle, transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus when present.
It is often absent on one or both sides.
The basiocciput gives attachment to the pharyngobasilar fascia at the pharyngeal tubercle

The pharyngeal tubercle on the basiocciput gives attachment to the pharyngobasilar fascia and the median raphe of the superior constrictor.
It is the top of the pharynx in the midline.
The alar ligaments attach to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum

The apical ligament attaches to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum (basion). The alar ligaments attach to the medial sides of the occipital condyles.
The alar ligaments limit rotation of the head.

questions.s: Concerning the lateral wall of the nasal cavity:
o: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus

The nasolacrimal duct opens into the anterior part of the inferior meatus, guarded by a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner).
Tears therefore drain into the nose.
The maxillary sinus opens into the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus

The maxillary ostium is high on the medial wall of the sinus and opens into the posterior part of the hiatus semilunaris in the middle meatus.
Because it is high, the sinus drains poorly by gravity.
The posterior ethmoidal air cells open into the middle meatus

The posterior ethmoidal cells open into the superior meatus. The anterior and middle cells open into the middle meatus.
The sphenoid sinus drains even higher, into the sphenoethmoidal recess.
The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess

The sphenoidal sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha.
This recess is a landmark for endoscopic access to the sphenoid.
The sphenoidal sinus is well developed at birth

The sphenoidal sinus is rudimentary at birth and develops mainly after puberty.
The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present (small) at birth.
The maxillary sinus opens into the inferior meatus

The maxillary sinus opens high on its medial wall into the posterior end of the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus.
Only the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.
The posterior ethmoidal air cells open into the middle meatus

The posterior ethmoidal cells open into the superior meatus.
The anterior and middle cells open into the middle meatus.
The infraorbital nerve runs in the roof of the maxillary sinus

The infraorbital nerve runs in its groove and canal in the floor of the orbit, which is the roof of the maxillary sinus.
Blow-out fractures of the orbital floor therefore cause numbness of the cheek.
